headings.title: Introduction to Lung Cancer in Community Health
headings.content: Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, presenting significant challenges in Nigerian community health nursing. In local primary and secondary healthcare settings, community health nurses frequently encounter patients presenting with advanced respiratory symptoms due to delayed diagnosis and limited access to specialized care. Understanding the epidemiological burden of lung cancer is essential for nursing students preparing for clinical practice and professional licensure examinations. This disease not only impacts the physical well-being of the affected individual but also places a heavy emotional and financial burden on families and the broader community. Furthermore, environmental exposures unique to various regions, such as the use of biomass fuels for indoor cooking and occupational hazards in mining or construction industries, contribute significantly to the local incidence of respiratory malignancies. Community health nurses play a pivotal role in bridging the gap between vulnerable populations and healthcare resources by advocating for early detection and comprehensive palliative care. By recognizing high-risk groups within the community, nurses can implement targeted educational interventions aimed at reducing exposure to known carcinogens. Addressing lung cancer from a public health perspective requires a multifaceted approach that integrates health promotion, risk reduction strategies, and culturally sensitive nursing interventions tailored to the Nigerian context.

headings.title: Risk Factors and Etiology of Lung Malignancies
headings.content: The etiology of lung cancer is multifactorial, involving a complex interplay between genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, and lifestyle choices. Cigarette smoking is by far the leading cause of lung malignancies, responsible for the vast majority of both small cell and non-small cell lung cancers. Tobacco smoke contains numerous chemical carcinogens, such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines, which induce deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) damage in the respiratory epithelium. However, nursing students must recognize that non-smokers can also develop lung cancer due to environmental and occupational risk factors. Radon gas exposure, secondhand smoke, air pollution, and occupational hazards such as asbestos, arsenic, nickel, and chromium significantly increase malignant transformation risks. In Nigeria and other developing regions, the reliance on biomass fuels for cooking and heating exposes individuals to indoor air pollution laden with particulate matter and toxic combustion byproducts, which poses an independent risk for lung carcinogenesis. Genetic susceptibility also plays a crucial role; individuals with a family history of lung cancer may harbor inherited mutations in tumor suppressor genes or DNA repair pathways that diminish their cellular defenses against carcinogens. Comprehensive nursing assessments must therefore encompass a detailed occupational, environmental, and smoking history to accurately evaluate a patient's cumulative risk profile and guide appropriate preventive counseling.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Major Classifications
headings.content: Lung cancers are broadly divided into two major histological classifications: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) and Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC). Understanding this classification is vital because treatment modalities and prognoses differ markedly between the two groups. NSCLC accounts for approximately 85% of all lung cancer cases and includes subtypes such as adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype found in non-smokers and typically arises in peripheral lung tissue, whereas squamous cell carcinoma is strongly linked to smoking and usually originates centrally in the major bronchi. SCLC accounts for the remaining 15% of cases and is characterized by its aggressive nature, rapid doubling time, and early dissemination to distant sites. SCLC is almost exclusively associated with heavy cigarette smoking and originates in the central airways, frequently exhibiting neuroendocrine features. The pathophysiology of lung cancer begins with chronic irritation and injury to the bronchial epithelium, leading to metaplasia, dysplasia, and eventually carcinoma in situ. Genetic mutations, including activation of oncogenes like K-ras and inactivation of tumor suppressor genes such as p53, drive uncontrolled cellular proliferation, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Nurses must understand these underlying cellular changes to comprehend why patients experience specific respiratory symptoms and how targeted pharmacological therapies work.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Symptom Recognition
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of lung cancer often develop insidiously, leading to delayed presentation where patients seek medical attention only when the disease has reached an advanced stage. Common local symptoms include a persistent, worsening cough that changes in character, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), dyspnea due to airway obstruction or pleural effusion, and recurring respiratory infections such as bronchitis or pneumonia distal to a blocked bronchus. Patients may also experience localized chest, shoulder, or back wall pain caused by direct pleural invasion or chest wall involvement. Systemic symptoms resulting from malignancy include unexplained weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, and cachexia. As the tumor grows or metastasizes, regional symptoms can emerge, such as hoarseness due to recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis, dysphagia from esophageal compression, and superior vena cava syndrome caused by vascular obstruction in the mediastinum. Additionally, lung cancers can manifest as paraneoplastic syndromes—disorders triggered by an immune response or ectopic hormone production by the tumor cells, such as syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) or hypercalcemia. Nurses must maintain a high index of suspicion when assessing patients with chronic respiratory complaints, ensuring thorough documentation and prompt referral for diagnostic evaluation.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Staging
headings.content: A systematic diagnostic evaluation is essential to confirm the presence of lung cancer, determine its exact histological type, and establish the extent of disease spread. The diagnostic workup typically begins with a chest radiograph, which may reveal pulmonary nodules, masses, or mediastinal widening, though computed tomography (CT) scans of the chest and upper abdomen provide much greater anatomical detail regarding tumor size, lymph node involvement, and distant metastases. Positron emission tomography (PET) scans are frequently utilized to assess metabolic activity in lesions and detect occult metastatic disease. Definitive diagnosis requires tissue acquisition for cytological or histological examination. Methods for obtaining tissue include sputum cytology, thoracentesis for malignant pleural effusions, CT-guided needle biopsy, and bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy or endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS). Once malignancy is confirmed, staging is performed to guide therapeutic decision-making. Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer is staged using the TNM system (Tumor, Node, Metastasis), which evaluates the primary tumor size, involvement of regional lymph nodes, and presence of distant metastases. Small Cell Lung Cancer is generally categorized simply as either 'limited stage' (confined to one hemithorax and safely encompassed within a radiation field) or 'extensive stage' (disseminated disease). Nurses play a vital role in preparing patients physically and psychologically for these diagnostic procedures, ensuring informed consent, and managing post-procedural recovery.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Management
headings.content: The medical and surgical management of lung cancer depends heavily on the histological classification, overall staging of the disease, and the patient's functional physiological status. For localized Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (stages I and II), surgical resection—ranging from wedge resection and segmentectomy to lobectomy or pneumonectomy—offers the best chance for cure. Thoracoscopic or robotic-assisted minimally invasive surgical approaches are increasingly utilized to reduce postoperative recovery time and complications. Adjuvant or neoadjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy may be combined with surgery to eradicate micro-metastases and shrink tumors prior to resection. For advanced NSCLC, treatment frequently incorporates molecular targeted therapies (such as epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors) and immunotherapy (immune checkpoint inhibitors), which have revolutionized oncology by specifically targeting tumor cells while sparing healthy tissue. In contrast, Small Cell Lung Cancer is treated primarily with systemic chemotherapy combined with concurrent or sequential thoracic radiation therapy, as SCLC is typically widely disseminated at diagnosis, rendering surgery rarely indicated except in very early, isolated cases. Palliative care is an integral component of management at all stages, focusing on relieving debilitating symptoms, maintaining quality of life, and supporting patients and their families through complex treatment trajectories.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Symptom Management
headings.content: Nursing care for patients with lung cancer requires a holistic, patient-centered approach aimed at optimizing physiological function, managing distressing symptoms, and providing psychosocial support. Nurses play a frontline role in monitoring respiratory status, administering prescribed oxygen therapy, teaching effective coughing and breathing exercises, and encouraging early ambulation to prevent atelectasis and pneumonia. Pain management is a cornerstone of oncology nursing; nurses must conduct regular pain assessments, administer analgesics according to the WHO pain ladder, and monitor for side effects such as opioid-induced constipation or respiratory depression. Nutritional support is equally crucial, as cancer cachexia and treatment side effects like nausea, vomiting, and mucositis impair oral intake; nurses can collaborate with dietitians to provide small, frequent, nutrient-dense meals and antiemetics as ordered. Furthermore, managing fatigue, alopecia, and the emotional distress of a cancer diagnosis requires empathetic communication, active listening, and referral to counseling or support groups. Nurses must also educate patients and caregivers on recognizing signs of complications, such as febrile neutropenia, worsening dyspnea, or acute hemoptysis, and provide clear instructions on when to seek immediate emergency medical evaluation.

headings.title: Prevention, Health Education, and Community Screening
headings.content: Prevention, health education, and community screening are powerful tools in reducing the global and local burden of lung cancer. Community health nurses occupy a strategic position to lead educational campaigns focused on smoking cessation, highlighting the dangers of tobacco use and exposure to secondhand smoke. In resource-constrained environments like Nigeria, educational initiatives must also address indoor air pollution by promoting improved ventilation practices and cleaner cooking technologies to minimize exposure to harmful biomass combustion fumes. Occupational health nurses play an essential role in enforcing safety regulations, ensuring that industrial workers utilize personal protective equipment such as specialized respirators to guard against asbestos, silica, and other airborne carcinogens. Regarding secondary prevention, low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening programs have demonstrated efficacy in detecting early-stage lung cancer among high-risk individuals, such as heavy, long-term smokers, significantly reducing mortality rates through timely intervention. Nurses are responsible for identifying eligible candidates for screening, explaining the benefits and potential risks (such as false positives and radiation exposure), and navigating patients through the follow-up diagnostic process. Ultimately, empowering communities through knowledge fosters proactive health behaviors and supports systemic policy changes aimed at eradicating preventable risk factors.
